result.issue: What can Cedar Lantern customers do with the billing export today, what are its current limits, and what is planned next?

questions.text: What can Cedar Lantern customers do with the billing export today, what are its current limits, and what is planned next?

answers.text:
Cedar Lantern customers can use the billing export to generate a CSV report showing completed appointments and associated charges for a selected month. The report includes the local appointment date, warehouse identifier, and charge amount. Account administrators can download this CSV to reconcile monthly invoices, though it is not a tax document and does not modify or pay invoices. The report is manually generated when the administrator requests it, so it may include corrections made after a prior download. Administrators can download prior closed months as well as the current month, though the current month may be incomplete until the month ends. The export is available to accounts on all paid plans, and only account administrators can generate it. Support can explain column meanings but cannot generate exports from the support console.
The current billing export has several limits. It is a manually downloaded CSV for one selected month, and only account administrators can generate it. A month may contain corrections made after a prior download. The export does not run on a schedule or send files by email, and it has no API. It cannot export more than one account at a time, and there is no plan to provide a combined multi-account report. The file is in the currency used on the invoice for the account, with no conversion column, and comparisons between accounts in different currencies must happen outside the product. The export does not support multiple accounts in the current screen.
The team plans to pilot scheduled email delivery with a small group in the third quarter of 2026. An export API is only under consideration; it is not approved or scheduled. The team has no commitment to provide a combined multi-account report, and no decision was made to introduce cross-account consolidation. The roadmap is a statement of intent and remains subject to engineering review, security review, and competing priorities. It is not evidence that a customer can use the feature today.

source_excerpts.quote: Cedar Lantern sells a warehouse scheduling service to distributors. Its billing export is a customer-controlled report rather than an accounting integration. Account administrators open Settings, select a month, and download a CSV showing completed appointments and the associated charge for each location. The export includes the local appointment date, warehouse identifier, and charge amount. The report is generated when the administrator requests it, so two downloads may differ if a completed

appointment was later corrected by the operations team. The CSV is intended to help finance teams reconcile a monthly invoice; it is not a tax document and does not itself pay or modify an invoice. Customers have asked for richer grouping, but the current interface has only the month selector and the location identifier in each row. Administrators can download prior closed months as well as the current month. The current month may be incomplete until the month ends. For internal

troubleshooting, support asks the administrator for the export month and account name rather than a copy of the entire file. The support team can compare the selected period with invoice line items and explain timing differences without making changes to the customer account.
- The current export is a manually downloaded CSV for one selected month.
- Only account administrators can generate it.
- A month may contain corrections made after a prior download.

The downloadable file is available to accounts on all paid plans. The permission check follows the current account administrator role, not the role of the person who originally created the account. Removing an administrator immediately removes their access to future downloads. Customer support can explain what each column means, but support staff cannot generate a customer export from the support console. For privacy, customer success should avoid asking users to email a full file; a redacted

example of an unexpected row is usually enough to investigate a discrepancy. Amounts are expressed in the currency used on the invoice for the account. The file has no conversion column, and any comparison between accounts in different currencies needs to happen outside the product. This matters for a distributor with several independently billed accounts, because each account generates its own report and has its own invoice. A user can reconcile those reports externally, but cannot select
multiple accounts in the current export screen.

The export does not run on a schedule or send files by email. It has no API and cannot export more than one account at a time. These are product limits as of this note, not temporary incidents or permission errors. The team has no commitment to provide a combined multi-account report.

The billing team reviewed requests from six account administrators who reconcile appointments against monthly invoices. Several wanted to receive an export without signing in on the first working day of each month. Others wanted the same rows to flow into their existing bookkeeping system. The team grouped these requests separately because delivery by email requires permissions and retention decisions, while a programmatic interface requires an authentication design and public documentation.

The team agreed that a missing feature should not be described as a customer-specific configuration issue. Support may share the current manual workflow and record the customer's desired delivery format, but should not promise an implementation date. No customer request in this review altered the current one-account scope, and no decision was made to introduce cross-account consolidation. The roadmap is a statement of intent and remains subject to engineering review, security review, and
competing priorities. It is not evidence that a customer can use the feature today.
The team plans to pilot scheduled email delivery with a small group in the third quarter of 2026. An export API is only under consideration; it is not approved or scheduled.

result.issue: How does Harbor Rivet handle a supplier safety incident from intake through closure, and who owns each stage and handoff?

questions.text: How does Harbor Rivet handle a supplier safety incident from intake through closure, and who owns each stage and handoff?

answers.text:
Harbor Rivet handles a supplier safety incident from intake through closure by following a structured process. The intake stage involves the person receiving the report recording the supplier, shipment identifiers, site, and available photographs in the incident register. Reports may come from various sources, including project sites, suppliers, the quality lab, or warehouse workers. The intake coordinator opens the incident record and places the affected shipment on hold, then hands the record and available evidence to the quality lead for assessment. A hold prevents further release of that shipment but does not automatically recall items already installed. After intake, the quality lead checks the affected lot against receiving records, identifies whether other shipments may contain the same material, and may request lab measurements or inspection certificates from the supplier. Missing certificates are logged as gaps rather than treated as proof that a part failed. When a lot cannot
who owns each stage and handoff. The intake coordinator owns the intake stage and hands off the incident record and evidence to the quality lead. The quality lead owns the assessment stage, checking the affected lot against receiving records and identifying other shipments. The quality lead also owns the decision about the affected scope and hands off the scoped list to the field safety manager to coordinate site action. The field safety manager owns the action and closure stage, contacting affected project sites and coordinating containment actions. The field safety manager records site acknowledgments and completed containment, then hands the action record back to the quality lead, who closes the incident after verifying actions and documenting follow-up. The quality lead owns the closure stage, ensuring that all actions are verified and documented.

source_excerpts.quote: Harbor Rivet buys fabricated metal fittings for commercial building projects. An incident is any report that a delivered fitting may create a safety risk, including a suspected material mix-up, an incomplete inspection record, or a physical failure in a field installation. The person receiving the report records the supplier, shipment identifiers, site, and available photographs in the incident register. Reports may come from a project site, a supplier, the quality lab, or a warehouse worker. A

report does not need a confirmed failure before it enters the register. The intake team avoids asking a field worker to remove a fitted part until site safety has assessed whether it is safe to do so. If there is a risk of immediate injury, the site follows its normal emergency procedure in parallel. The register should capture the first notification time and any gaps in shipment identification so that quality can request the missing information later. Customer names are recorded in the
restricted register, not in the general supplier channel.

The intake coordinator opens the incident record and places the affected shipment on hold. The coordinator then hands the record and available evidence to the quality lead for assessment. A hold prevents further release of that shipment; it does not automatically recall items already installed.

After intake, the quality lead checks the affected lot against the receiving records and identifies whether other shipments may contain the same material. The lead may request lab measurements or inspection certificates from the supplier. Missing certificates are logged as gaps rather than treated as proof that a part failed. When a lot cannot be identified, the lead records the uncertainty and asks the warehouse to preserve the relevant delivery records. The assessment distinguishes items

still in Harbor Rivet custody from items already delivered to a project site; these groups need different follow-up. Quality records its reasoning and any unresolved evidence in the same restricted incident register. A hold stays in place during assessment unless an authorized quality decision changes it. The supplier can supply evidence, but its proposed interpretation does not by itself release material. The lead also checks whether a similar report exists for a different supplier and keeps
unrelated reports separate unless a real common cause is established.

The quality lead decides the affected scope and documents the evidence and uncertainties. For any material already delivered, the quality lead hands the scoped list to the field safety manager to coordinate site action. The decision about a customer site is not delegated to the intake coordinator.

The field safety manager contacts the affected project sites identified by quality and agrees safe inspection or containment actions with the responsible site contacts. For products still in the warehouse, quality coordinates with warehouse operations on segregation and any further testing. Site actions should record who was contacted, the date of contact, and whether a site has acknowledged the proposed action. A site may need additional time to obtain access or a specialist inspection, so

contact alone is not the same as completed containment. The manager flags unresponsive sites to the incident review meeting rather than assuming that the work is complete. Supporting material is retained in the restricted register and any corrections to a lot identifier are explained in the record. Supplier response documents are attached with their date, and any open technical question remains visible to the quality lead. The company does not require removal of every delivered part when
assessment supports a narrower response.

evidence.heading: Supplier incident playbook — section 1: intake
evidence.content:
Harbor Rivet buys fabricated metal fittings for commercial building projects. An incident is any report that a delivered fitting may create a safety risk, including a suspected material mix-up, an incomplete inspection record, or a physical failure in a field installation. The person receiving the report records the supplier, shipment identifiers, site, and available photographs in the incident register. Reports may come from a project site, a supplier, the quality lab, or a warehouse worker. A report does not need a confirmed failure before it enters the register. The intake team avoids asking a field worker to remove a fitted part until site safety has assessed whether it is safe to do so. If there is a risk of immediate injury, the site follows its normal emergency procedure in parallel. The register should capture the first notification time and any gaps in shipment identification so that quality can request the missing information later. Customer names are recorded in the restricted register, not in the general supplier channel.

The intake coordinator opens the incident record and places the affected shipment on hold. The coordinator then hands the record and available evidence to the quality lead for assessment. A hold prevents further release of that shipment; it does not automatically recall items already installed.

evidence.heading: Supplier incident playbook — section 2: assessment
evidence.content:
After intake, the quality lead checks the affected lot against the receiving records and identifies whether other shipments may contain the same material. The lead may request lab measurements or inspection certificates from the supplier. Missing certificates are logged as gaps rather than treated as proof that a part failed. When a lot cannot be identified, the lead records the uncertainty and asks the warehouse to preserve the relevant delivery records. The assessment distinguishes items still in Harbor Rivet custody from items already delivered to a project site; these groups need different follow-up. Quality records its reasoning and any unresolved evidence in the same restricted incident register. A hold stays in place during assessment unless an authorized quality decision changes it. The supplier can supply evidence, but its proposed interpretation does not by itself release material. The lead also checks whether a similar report exists for a different supplier and keeps unrelated reports separate unless a real common cause is established.

The quality lead decides the affected scope and documents the evidence and uncertainties. For any material already delivered, the quality lead hands the scoped list to the field safety manager to coordinate site action. The decision about a customer site is not delegated to the intake coordinator.

evidence.heading: Supplier incident playbook — section 3: action and closure
evidence.content:
The field safety manager contacts the affected project sites identified by quality and agrees safe inspection or containment actions with the responsible site contacts. For products still in the warehouse, quality coordinates with warehouse operations on segregation and any further testing. Site actions should record who was contacted, the date of contact, and whether a site has acknowledged the proposed action. A site may need additional time to obtain access or a specialist inspection, so contact alone is not the same as completed containment. The manager flags unresponsive sites to the incident review meeting rather than assuming that the work is complete. Supporting material is retained in the restricted register and any corrections to a lot identifier are explained in the record. Supplier response documents are attached with their date, and any open technical question remains visible to the quality lead. The company does not require removal of every delivered part when assessment supports a narrower response.

The field safety manager records site acknowledgments and completed containment, then hands the action record back to the quality lead. The quality lead closes the incident only after verifying the actions and documenting any remaining follow-up owner. Closing the register entry is an administrative decision and does not erase the evidence.

evidence.heading: Follow-up support report — March 2026 cohort
evidence.content:
The report includes cases submitted from March 1 through March 31 and resolved by the reporting cutoff. Operations used the same version 3 definition and event-log extraction as for the January baseline. A new routing queue was introduced between the periods, but the comparison alone does not establish that the queue caused the observed change. Changes in the mix of customer questions, staffing, or the number of cases still open at cutoff may also influence the published median. The team maintained a separate table of open cases and did not assign those cases an artificial resolution duration. For this report, standard priority is the priority recorded at submission, so an agent's later change to a ticket's label does not retrospectively put it in or out of the cohort. Customers' names were removed from the aggregate report before the results were shared with the product team. Each report describes submitted cases from its own month, rather than the exact same tickets followed across both months. March is the after period in the improvement review.

The March cohort's median business time to first resolution was 3.75 business days. The report compares this median with the January median of 5 business days, using January as the baseline.

evidence.heading: Baseline support report — January 2026 cohort
evidence.content:
The report includes cases submitted from January 1 through January 31 and resolved by the reporting cutoff. The support team applied the version 3 metric definition consistently to this cohort before publishing it. Case submission times and resolution times came from the support system's event log, and the operations analyst checked the resulting duration distribution for duplicate records. Internal training exercises were tagged before extraction so they did not enter the cohort. The cohort was not restricted to a single day of the week or to a single support agent, and it covers standard-priority cases from paying repair shops. The published value is a median across the qualifying individual cases. It is not a target or a guaranteed maximum for an individual customer. The report includes a separate open-case count, because excluding unresolved cases means the median does not describe how long those outstanding cases will eventually take. The team cautions against comparing this figure to an elapsed-clock-time metric without conversion. January is the before period in the improvement review.

The January cohort's median business time to first resolution was 5 business days. This baseline uses the same case definition as the later March cohort.

evidence.heading: Support measurement specification — version 3
evidence.content:
Copper Wren provides workflow software for independent repair shops. The support operations team publishes a monthly duration measure to understand how long ordinary cases take to resolve. Each observation starts when a customer submits a new support case and ends at the first time that case is marked resolved by an agent. If a resolved case is later reopened, the initial resolution timestamp remains the endpoint of this measure. The team uses business time rather than elapsed clock time, counting eight working hours per business day and excluding nights and weekends. The median is calculated across case-level durations, not by taking the mean of daily medians. Cases are grouped by the month in which they were submitted, and the calculation is rerun after the follow-up period has ended so that late resolutions can be counted. Cases that remain unresolved at the cutoff are handled under a separate open-case report and do not enter the resolved-case median. This metric is intended to describe speed for this narrowly defined case population; it is not a measure of customer satisfaction or engineering delivery time.

The measurement covers standard-priority support cases submitted by paying repair shops. It excludes urgent cases, internal test tickets, and cases unresolved at the reporting cutoff. Business time excludes nights and weekends and counts eight working hours per business day.
